title: Aristotle's Ethics
orientation: This chapter examines the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle's systematic account of virtue, happiness, and the good life, which Russell reads as expressing the settled opinions of a well-off, educated Greek gentleman rather than any mystical or revolutionary vision. Understanding it matters both as a landmark of systematic moral philosophy (the doctrine of the golden mean, the analysis of virtue and happiness) and as a case study, for Russell, in how far a philosopher's ethics can be internally consistent and yet still strike a later age as morally impoverished.
historical_background: Of the three ethical treatises attributed to Aristotle, two are now generally held to be by disciples; Russell follows convention in treating the Nicomachean Ethics as authentically Aristotle's, while noting scholarly doubt about Books V-VII. The work reflects the outlook of a leisured, aristocratic Athenian society resting on slavery and the subordination of women, in which 'the good life' was assumed to require external goods, high birth, and freedom from manual labour.
philosophical_problems: What is happiness, and is it the same as pleasure?
Can every virtue really be analysed as a mean between two vicious extremes?
Does justice mean equality, or proportion according to merit?
Is the highest good available only to a few (the philosopher, the magnanimous man), or must ethics apply equally to everyone?
How should we judge an ancient ethical theory: by its internal consistency, its consistency with the author's other views, or by whether it matches our own moral feelings?

philosophers_discussed.name: Aristotle
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Author of the Nicomachean Ethics; Russell reconstructs his account of happiness, virtue, the golden mean, justice, friendship, pleasure, and contemplation, and closes with a sustained critical evaluation of the whole work.

philosophers_discussed.name: Plato
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as the source of the tripartite division of the soul (rational and irrational, the latter further divided into vegetative and appetitive) that Aristotle adopts, and as holding the more mystical, ascetic view of pleasure that Aristotle's more moderate treatment implicitly corrects.

philosophers_discussed.name: Kant
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited for the view that every human being is an end in himself, taken by Russell as an expression of the Christian-derived alternative to Aristotle's and Plato's acceptance of inequality; Russell notes a logical difficulty in Kant's view when two people's interests as 'ends in themselves' clash.

philosophers_discussed.name: Bentham
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited, with 'the utilitarians,' as interpreting justice as equality: when interests clash, the right course maximizes total happiness regardless of who enjoys it, in contrast to Aristotle's proportional conception of justice.

philosophers_discussed.name: Nietzsche
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Mentioned as agreeing with Plato and Aristotle that the best things in life should be confined to a few, and as having called Christian ethics a 'slave-morality' -- a judgement Russell says Aristotle's portrait of the magnanimous man helps to justify.

schools_discussed: Stoicism and early Christianity (contrasted briefly as holding virtue possible for slaves as much as masters)
Utilitarianism (Bentham, contrasted on the meaning of justice)

core_concepts.name: Happiness as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue
core_concepts.plain_explanation: For Aristotle, being happy is not a passive feeling but a matter of actively living and acting well, exercising your best capacities, over a complete life.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's central ethical claim that 'the good' is happiness (eudaimonia), and that happiness consists in 'activity of soul in accordance with virtue in a complete life,' with the rational soul's contemplative activity representing its highest and most complete form.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It makes Aristotle's ethics teleological (aimed at a final good) rather than rule-based, and ties ethical theory directly to his metaphysical account of the soul and its rational and irrational parts.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Set out at the start of the Nicomachean Ethics.
examples: The claim that a man cannot be called happy 'on the rack,' since some degree of external good fortune is necessary for happiness
competing_positions: Those who regard pleasure itself, rather than virtuous activity, as the good, and so treat virtue purely as a means
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Provides the ethical foundation for the later doctrines of the golden mean and of contemplation as the highest happiness.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Because Aristotle considers ethics a branch of politics, this definition of happiness underlies his views on the best form of government.

core_concepts.name: The doctrine of the golden mean
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Every virtue, Aristotle argues, lies at a mid-point between two opposite vices -- one of excess, one of deficiency. Courage, for example, is the mean between the excess of rashness and the deficiency of cowardice.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that moral virtue is a disposition to feel and act in a way that is intermediate between two vicious extremes, one of excess and one of deficiency, relative to the particular person and situation -- e.g. courage between cowardice and rashness, liberality between prodigality and meanness, proper pride between vanity and humility.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It became the most famous and influential single doctrine of Aristotle's ethics, offering a systematic method for identifying virtues by locating the extremes on either side of them.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed across Books II-IV of the Nicomachean Ethics.
examples: Courage as the mean between cowardice and rashness
Liberality as the mean between prodigality and meanness
Ready wit as the mean between buffoonery and boorishness
Truthfulness (about oneself) as the mean between boastfulness and mock-modesty
objections: Russell notes the scheme does not obviously fit truthfulness in any wider sense than truthfulness about oneself, and mocks a real-life mayor who claimed to have steered a mean between 'partiality' and 'impartiality'
It cannot apply to intellectual contemplation, which the Ethics elsewhere calls the best of all activities -- there being no vice of 'excess' of contemplation on Aristotle's own account
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Became a standard reference point in virtue ethics down to the present.

core_concepts.name: The magnanimous (great-souled) man
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Aristotle's portrait of the ideal proud man: someone who knows his own great worth, expects and only moderately accepts honour, disdains danger and dishonour, is generous but ashamed to receive favours, and moves and speaks with slow, dignified deliberateness.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's description of megalopsychia ('great-souledness,' rendered 'magnanimous' by Russell rather than 'proud'): the crowning virtue that presupposes and enhances all the others, concerned chiefly with great honours and dishonours, and possible in practice only for someone of exceptional social position, wealth, and virtue.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats it as showing, more vividly than any argument, the gulf between pagan and Christian ethics, since the magnanimous man's studied pride, disdain, and self-sufficiency are close to what Christianity would call sinful vanity.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Described at length in Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (1123b-1125a).
examples: The magnanimous man is 'apt to confer greater benefits in return' so as to remain the superior party in an exchange
He 'does not run into trifling dangers... but will face great dangers,' being unsparing of his life when the cause is worthy
He has a 'slow step,' a 'deep voice,' and 'a level utterance'
objections: Russell remarks that 'one shudders to think what a vain man would be like' if this figure represents the virtuous mean
competing_positions: Christian humility, which treats as a virtue precisely what Aristotle treats as a vice (self-effacement), and treats pride, which Aristotle praises, as a sin -- Russell links this to Nietzsche's charge that Christianity is a 'slave-morality'
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Illustrates, for Russell, why the highest Aristotelian virtue can exist only for a small, socially privileged minority, tying his ethics directly to his preference for monarchy and aristocracy in politics.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political: 'there cannot be very many' magnanimous men in a community, since the virtue presupposes an exceptional social position.

core_concepts.name: Justice as proportion rather than equality
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Rather than everyone deserving an equal share, Aristotle thinks justice means each person getting a share appropriate to their own worth or merit -- so unequal shares can still be just.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's view that justice involves 'not equality, but right proportion, which is only sometimes equality,' so that, for example, the superior in an unequal relationship (husband, parent, master) may rightly receive more honour or love than they give, and political power may rightly be distributed unevenly according to virtue.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It underlies Aristotle's acceptance of slavery, the subordination of women and children, and his preference for aristocracy and monarchy, and sets up Russell's later contrast with modern egalitarian conceptions of justice.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed in Nicomachean Ethics V, and applied throughout the Ethics to household and political relationships.
examples: A father may repudiate a wicked son, but a son cannot repudiate his father, since he owes him more than he can repay
In marriage, 'the man rules... but the matters that befit a woman he hands over to her'
There can be no injustice to one's own property, including, in this framework, one's slave or son
objections: Russell notes Aristotle 'never seems to have realized the difficulty' that 'proportion' must track virtue, which is hard to measure and a matter of party controversy, so in practice it collapses into proportion by wealth
competing_positions: Kant's view that every human being is an end in himself
Bentham and the utilitarians' view that justice means treating everyone's happiness equally, regardless of merit
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Frames the long historical contest, which Russell traces down to Kant and Bentham, over whether justice means equality or desert-based proportion.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political and, in its origin, religious: Russell notes the Greek idea of each person having a 'proper sphere' derives from primitive religion.

core_concepts.name: Contemplation as the highest happiness
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Of all human activities, Aristotle holds that pure intellectual contemplation -- thinking for its own sake -- is the best and happiest, because it is most godlike and requires the least dependence on external circumstances.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's culminating doctrine that perfect happiness lies in the best activity, contemplation, since it alone offers leisure and is 'preferable to war or politics or any other practical career'; the philosopher, being most akin to God in exercising reason, is 'the dearest to the gods' and therefore the happiest of men.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is, in Russell's assessment, 'the only doctrine in the book which is not mere common sense,' distinguishing Aristotle's ethics from a merely conventional restatement of respectable Athenian opinion.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Set out near the close of the Nicomachean Ethics (Book X).
examples: The claim that 'the activity of God, which surpasses all others in blessedness, must be contemplative'
objections: Russell notes this doctrine sits awkwardly with the golden mean, since no vicious 'excess' of contemplation is identified
competing_positions: Practical, active life (politics, war) as the highest good, which Aristotle explicitly ranks below contemplation
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Links ethics to Aristotle's theology, since contemplation is the one respect in which men 'share in the divine life.'

arguments.title: Every virtue is a mean between two vicious extremes
premises: Examination of particular virtues shows each flanked by two corresponding vices, one of excess and one of deficiency.
Courage lies between cowardice (deficiency) and rashness (excess); liberality between meanness and prodigality; proper pride between humility and vanity; wit between boorishness and buffoonery.
arguments.conclusion: Moral virtue in general is a mean state between two extremes, each of which is a vice.
arguments.explanation: Aristotle generalizes from a survey of specific virtue-pairs to a systematic doctrine intended to cover moral virtue as such.
objections: Russell notes truthfulness fits awkwardly (Aristotle restricts it to truthfulness about oneself) and intellectual contemplation, elsewhere called the best activity, does not fit the scheme at all
The doctrine could be maintained by restricting it to practical (not intellectual) virtues, which Russell allows as a possible defense
implications: Establishes the golden mean as Aristotle's central practical-ethical method, while leaving its scope over intellectual virtue unresolved

arguments.title: The legislator's task of habituating citizens to virtue
premises: Moral virtues, unlike intellectual ones, result from habit rather than teaching.
We become just by performing just acts, and similarly for other virtues.
By being compelled to acquire good habits, citizens will in time come to find pleasure in virtuous action.
arguments.conclusion: It is the legislator's business to make citizens good by forming good habits through law and compulsion, which will eventually produce genuine, pleasurable virtue rather than mere compliance.
arguments.explanation: This grounds Aristotle's view of ethics as continuous with politics: character is shaped by the community's laws and institutions, not simply chosen by isolated individuals.
objections: Russell points out the legislator could equally cause the young to acquire bad habits; avoiding this requires the legislator to have 'all the wisdom of a Platonic guardian,' and if such wisdom is lacking, the promised pleasure in virtue may never materialize
implications: Ties the success of Aristotle's ethical theory to unresolved political questions about who legislates and how wisely

arguments.title: Ethics is subordinate to politics because the good community may require subordination
premises: The highest good aimed at is the good of the whole community, not merely of separate individuals.
In an organized whole (Aristotle's analogy: an orchestra), some parts are necessarily more important than others for the excellence of the whole.
It is impossible to organize such a whole purely by giving each member what would be best for him considered in isolation.
arguments.conclusion: A good community may legitimately be one containing subordination -- some citizens (the magnanimous, the philosophically gifted) properly enjoying more of the highest goods than others.
arguments.explanation: This argument connects Aristotle's ethics of unequal desert to his political preference for monarchy and aristocracy, treating the community, not the isolated individual, as the primary unit of ethical evaluation.
objections: Russell notes this raises, but does not resolve, the deeper question of whether social good is simply the sum of individual goods or something belonging to the whole as such -- a question later pressed by Hegelian philosophers
implications: Even modern democracies, Russell observes, implicitly accept a version of this by expecting more of Presidents or Prime Ministers than of ordinary citizens

arguments.title: Russell's three-question test for evaluating Aristotle's ethics
premises: Any ethical theory can be asked: (1) Is it internally self-consistent? (2) Is it consistent with the rest of the author's philosophy? (3) Does it answer ethical problems in a way consonant with our own ethical feelings?
A negative answer to (1) or (2) shows an intellectual error; a negative answer to (3) shows only disagreement of taste, not error.
arguments.conclusion: Applied to Aristotle: the Ethics is largely self-consistent (aside from the golden mean's difficulty with intellectual virtue and an ambiguity about the legislator), fully consistent with his teleological metaphysics, but strikingly at odds with modern sentiment on equality, benevolence, and the treatment of slaves and women.
arguments.explanation: This three-part test lets Russell separate genuine philosophical error from mere disagreement in values, and is his explicit method for structuring the chapter's closing evaluation of Aristotle.
implications: Allows Russell to say Aristotle's ethics is not simply 'wrong,' the way his astronomy is, since ethics (unlike astronomy) has made no scientifically ascertained progress -- but it can still be judged emotionally impoverished

key_distinctions: Intellectual virtue (from teaching) vs. moral virtue (from habit)
Virtue as a mean vs. the two flanking vicious extremes (excess and deficiency)
Justice as proportion (Aristotle, ancient Greek view) vs. justice as equality (Kant's 'end in himself'; Bentham's utilitarian equal-weighing of happiness)
Virtue as a means to happiness vs. virtue (especially the intellectual virtues) as itself part of the end
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Aristotle explicitly follows Plato in dividing the soul into rational and irrational parts, the irrational further divided into vegetative and appetitive; but, Russell notes, Aristotle's ethics lacks the 'mystical religion' and unorthodox proposals about property and the family found in Plato's Republic.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell traces the later historical divide over Aristotle's proportional justice down to Kant (every human being an end in himself) and Bentham and the utilitarians (justice as equal weighing of happiness), and links Aristotle's acceptance of a hierarchy of merit to Nietzsche's approval of inequality and his critique of Christianity as a 'slave-morality.'
political_social_context: Aristotle treats ethics as a branch of politics; his acceptance of slavery, the subordination of women and children, and his preference for monarchy and aristocracy over democracy are presented as continuous with, not incidental to, his ethical theory of proportional justice and the magnanimous man.
religion_science_culture_context: Russell contrasts Aristotle's ethics with the Stoic-Christian view that virtue is possible equally for slave and master, noting that Christian ethics reverses Aristotle's evaluation of pride (a vice for Christians, a virtue for Aristotle) and humility (a virtue for Christians, near-vice for Aristotle), citing Pope Gregory the Great's reproof of a bishop for teaching grammar as an example of the later devaluation of intellectual virtue.
russell_presentation: Russell presents the Nicomachean Ethics as a systematic but essentially conventional restatement of the moral outlook of 'decent, well-behaved' educated Greek men of Aristotle's own class and time, appealing to 'the respectable middle-aged' rather than offering anything to those 'possessed by a god or a devil.' He carefully reconstructs the doctrine of happiness as virtuous activity, the golden mean, the account of justice as proportion, the extended portrait of the magnanimous man, the discussions of friendship and pleasure, and the culminating claim that contemplative activity is the highest happiness -- noting this last point as the one place the book rises above mere common sense. He then applies his own three-part test (internal consistency, consistency with Aristotle's metaphysics, and agreement with modern moral feeling) and concludes the book is largely self-consistent and fully consistent with Aristotle's teleological metaphysics, but is severely wanting by modern standards: it accepts inequality (slavery, the subjection of women, a virtue reserved for the socially exceptional few) that Russell finds 'repugnant,' and displays what he calls an 'emotional poverty' and 'almost complete absence... of benevolence or philanthropy.' His final verdict is unusually blunt: 'his Ethics, in spite of its fame, is lacking in intrinsic importance.'
critical_context: Common scholarly caveat: many later moral philosophers, particularly in the twentieth-century revival of virtue ethics (e.g., in the tradition running through Anscombe and MacIntyre), have judged the Nicomachean Ethics far more favourably than Russell does here, treating its account of character, practical wisdom, and the mean as a serious and still-useful alternative to both Kantian and utilitarian ethics, rather than as merely a 'smug' restatement of conventional Athenian opinion.
key_takeaways: Aristotle defines the good as happiness, understood as virtuous activity of the soul over a complete life, with contemplation as its highest form.

The doctrine of the golden mean holds that every (practical) virtue is a mean between two vicious extremes of excess and deficiency, though Russell notes it does not obviously fit intellectual contemplation or truthfulness in the widest sense.
Aristotle's magnanimous (great-souled) man -- proud, self-sufficient, disdainful of trivial honours -- vividly illustrates, for Russell, the gulf between pagan and Christian ethics.

Aristotle holds that justice means proportion according to merit, not equality, which underlies his acceptance of slavery and the subordination of women, and which Russell contrasts with Kant's and Bentham's more egalitarian conceptions.

Applying his own three-part test, Russell judges the Ethics largely self-consistent and consistent with Aristotle's metaphysics, but morally impoverished by modern standards -- lacking benevolence and emotional depth.
Russell's overall verdict is that the Nicomachean Ethics, despite its fame, is 'lacking in intrinsic importance.'
study_notes:
The most useful analytic tool in this chapter is Russell's three-question test for judging any ethical theory: is it internally consistent, is it consistent with the philosopher's other commitments, and does it match our own moral feelings? Notice that Russell treats only the first two as questions of genuine philosophical error; a negative answer to the third tells us only that we disagree with the philosopher's values, not that the philosopher has made a mistake. This distinction is a good general-purpose tool for reading any historical ethical text without either dismissing it anachronistically or excusing everything in it as 'a product of its time.'

Watch, too, how the golden mean, justice as proportion, and the magnanimous man all connect back to the same underlying commitment: that the highest human goods are naturally and rightly available only to a socially exceptional few. This is why Russell treats Aristotle's ethics and politics as continuous rather than separate subjects -- the claim that virtue is a mean, applied to pride specifically, generates a character sketch (the magnanimous man) that only makes sense for someone already wealthy, well-born, and powerful, which in turn only makes sense within a political order (aristocracy or monarchy) that reserves the best things for the few.

Finally, notice the asymmetry in Russell's own judgement: he finds the doctrine of contemplation as the highest happiness intellectually the most interesting part of the book, yet still delivers a harsh final verdict on the whole work, based not on any logical flaw but on what he calls its 'emotional poverty' -- a reminder that a philosopher can pass every test of consistency and still be judged, on humane grounds, to have missed something important.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: For Aristotle, not just a feeling of pleasure but living and acting well -- exercising your best abilities over the course of a whole life.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's term for the highest human good, defined as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a complete life, with contemplative activity as its most perfect form.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that every virtue is a balanced middle point between two bad extremes -- for example, courage is the balance between cowardice and recklessness.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's doctrine that moral virtue is a disposition intermediate between two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency, relative to the agent and situation.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Aristotle's picture of the ideally proud man -- dignified, self-sufficient, only moderately pleased by honours, and contemptuous of trivial concerns.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The virtue Aristotle treats as the 'crown' of the other virtues, presupposing exceptional social position and worth, and concerned chiefly with the proper attitude toward honour and dishonour.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that fairness means giving each person what fits their own worth or merit, not necessarily the same as everyone else.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's view that justice consists in proportionate rather than strictly equal distribution, applied to relationships of unequal worth such as master/slave, parent/child, husband/wife.

questions.prompt: How does Aristotle define happiness, and what activity does he consider its highest form?
questions.answer: Happiness is 'activity of soul in accordance with virtue in a complete life.' Its highest form is contemplation, the exercise of reason for its own sake, because it is most godlike and offers the most leisure.
questions.explanation: This is the organizing definition for the rest of the Ethics as Russell presents it.

questions.prompt: Give three examples of virtues Aristotle analyses as a mean between two vices, naming the flanking extremes.
questions.answer: Courage, between cowardice (deficiency) and rashness (excess); liberality, between meanness (deficiency) and prodigality (excess); proper pride, between humility (deficiency) and vanity (excess).
questions.explanation: The golden mean is Aristotle's central method for analysing practical virtue.

questions.prompt: Compare Aristotle's conception of justice as proportion with Kant's and Bentham's conceptions, as Russell presents them.
questions.answer: Aristotle holds that justice is proportion according to merit, not equality -- so unequal shares of honour, power, or love can be just if they track real differences of worth. Kant holds every human being is an end in himself, implying a basic equality of moral status, though Russell notes this leaves unclear how to adjudicate when two such 'ends in themselves' conflict. Bentham and the utilitarians interpret justice as equality: the right action maximizes total happiness regardless of who receives it, rewarding virtue only instrumentally, for its long-run social benefit, not because the virtuous inherently deserve more.
questions.explanation: This threefold contrast is Russell's main device for situating Aristotle's ethics relative to modern moral philosophy.

questions.prompt: What objection does Russell raise against Aristotle's claim that the legislator can reliably make citizens virtuous through habituation?
questions.answer: The legislator could equally cause the young to acquire bad habits; avoiding this requires the legislator to possess all the wisdom of a Platonic guardian, and if this wisdom is lacking, Aristotle's claim that habituated virtue eventually becomes pleasurable may simply fail.
questions.explanation: Russell treats this as a real but perhaps more political than ethical difficulty in Aristotle's account.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's three-part test for evaluating an ethical theory and state his verdict on each part as applied to Aristotle.
questions.answer: The three questions are: (1) Is the theory internally self-consistent? (2) Is it consistent with the rest of the philosopher's views? (3) Does it match our own ethical feelings? Russell judges Aristotle's Ethics largely self-consistent (with minor difficulties around the golden mean and the legislator), fully consistent with his teleological metaphysics, but sharply at odds with modern sentiment regarding equality, slavery, and benevolence.
questions.explanation: Only a negative answer to the first two questions indicates a philosophical error, in Russell's framework; disagreement on the third indicates only a difference in values.

questions.prompt: What overall verdict does Russell reach on the Nicomachean Ethics, and on what grounds?
questions.answer: Russell judges the Ethics 'lacking in intrinsic importance' despite its fame, on the grounds of its 'emotional poverty' and 'almost complete absence... of benevolence or philanthropy' -- it speaks only to comfortable men of moderate passions and has nothing for those in genuine despair or moral crisis.
questions.explanation: Notably, this is a moral/emotional judgement, not a claim of logical inconsistency, consistent with Russell's own three-part evaluative framework.

flashcards.front: What is the good, according to Aristotle's Ethics?
flashcards.back: Happiness (eudaimonia), understood as activity of soul in accordance with virtue in a complete life.

flashcards.front: What two parts does Aristotle, following Plato, divide the soul into?
flashcards.back: A rational part and an irrational part; the irrational part is further divided into the vegetative (found even in plants) and the appetitive (found in all animals).

flashcards.front: What is the doctrine of the golden mean?
flashcards.back: Every moral virtue is a mean between two vicious extremes, one of excess and one of deficiency.

flashcards.front: Name the mean and the two extremes for courage.
flashcards.back: Courage is the mean between cowardice (deficiency) and rashness (excess).

flashcards.front: What difficulty does Russell note in fitting truthfulness into the golden mean scheme?
flashcards.back: Aristotle's mean (between boastfulness and mock-modesty) only covers truthfulness about oneself, not truthfulness in the wider sense.

flashcards.front: What does Aristotle mean by saying justice is 'proportion' rather than 'equality'?
flashcards.back: Fair shares should track each person's worth or merit, so unequal treatment (e.g. of master and slave, or husband and wife) can still be just.
Aristotle's portrait of the ideally proud, self-sufficient man, concerned chiefly with great honours, who disdains trifling dangers and dishonours and confers benefits rather than receiving them.

flashcards.front: What does Nietzsche's phrase 'slave-morality' refer to, in this context?
flashcards.back: His characterization of Christian ethics, which praises humility (a near-vice for Aristotle) and condemns pride (a virtue for Aristotle) -- illustrated for Russell by the magnanimous man.

flashcards.front: What activity does Aristotle call the highest and happiest human activity?
flashcards.back: Contemplation -- pure intellectual activity for its own sake, most akin to the activity of God.

flashcards.front: According to Kant, as cited by Russell, what is every human being?
flashcards.back: An end in himself -- though Russell notes this leaves unresolved how to decide between two people's competing claims as 'ends in themselves.'

flashcards.front: How do Bentham and the utilitarians define justice, in contrast to Aristotle?
flashcards.back: As equality: maximizing total happiness regardless of who enjoys it, rather than proportion according to merit.

flashcards.front: What objection does Russell raise to Aristotle's claim that a legislator can reliably instill virtuous habits?
flashcards.back: The legislator could equally instill bad habits; avoiding this requires all the wisdom of a Platonic guardian.

flashcards.front: What are Russell's three questions for evaluating any ethical theory?
flashcards.back: (1) Is it self-consistent? (2) Is it consistent with the philosopher's other views? (3) Does it match our own ethical feelings?

flashcards.front: What is Russell's final verdict on the Nicomachean Ethics?
flashcards.back: That it is 'lacking in intrinsic importance,' due to its emotional poverty and near-total absence of benevolence or philanthropy.

quiz.prompt: What does Aristotle identify as 'the good' at the start of the Ethics?
options: Happiness, as an activity of the soul
quiz.explanation: Aristotle defines the good as happiness, understood as virtuous activity of the soul.
quiz.related_concept: Happiness as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue

quiz.prompt: According to the golden mean, courage is the mean between which two extremes?
quiz.explanation: Courage lies between the deficiency of cowardice and the excess of rashness.
quiz.related_concept: The doctrine of the golden mean

quiz.prompt: Russell notes that the doctrine of the golden mean applies smoothly to intellectual contemplation, which Aristotle elsewhere calls the best of all activities.
quiz.explanation: Russell points out the mean scheme does not obviously apply to contemplation, since no vicious 'excess' of it is identified.
quiz.related_concept: The doctrine of the golden mean

quiz.prompt: What does Aristotle mean by holding that justice is 'proportion' rather than 'equality'?
options: Everyone should receive exactly equal shares
Fair shares should track each person's merit or worth, so unequal treatment can be just
Justice applies only to citizens, never to slaves or family members
Justice is entirely a matter of legal statute
quiz.explanation: Aristotle's proportional conception underlies his acceptance of unequal treatment within households and the state.
quiz.related_concept: Justice as proportion rather than equality

quiz.prompt: Which virtue does Aristotle describe as the 'crown' of the other virtues, presupposing an exceptional social position?
quiz.explanation: The magnanimous man's virtue depends on wealth, birth, and honour that only a few can possess.

quiz.prompt: How do Bentham and the utilitarians, as cited by Russell, differ from Aristotle on the meaning of justice?
options: They deny that justice is a virtue at all
They hold justice means maximizing total happiness regardless of who enjoys it, rather than proportion according to merit
They agree entirely with Aristotle's proportional view
They hold justice is purely a matter of divine command
quiz.explanation: Utilitarian justice weighs everyone's happiness equally; Aristotle's proportional justice rewards greater merit with a greater share.
quiz.related_concept: Justice as proportion rather than equality

quiz.prompt: Aristotle holds that the highest and happiest human activity is ____, because it is most akin to the activity of God.
quiz.explanation: Contemplative activity is ranked above practical or political activity as the peak of human happiness.

quiz.prompt: What is Russell's final verdict on the Nicomachean Ethics, and on what basis?
options: That it is logically inconsistent throughout
That it is 'lacking in intrinsic importance,' due to emotional poverty and near-absence of benevolence
That it is superior to all modern ethical theories
That it was not written by Aristotle at all
quiz.explanation: Russell's judgement rests on moral/emotional grounds -- via his own third evaluative question -- not on internal inconsistency.

essay_prompts.prompt: Using Russell's own three-question framework (internal consistency, consistency with the author's broader philosophy, agreement with our own ethical feelings), evaluate Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics as presented in this chapter.
rubric: Applies each question to specific features of Aristotle's ethics (golden mean, justice as proportion, the magnanimous man)
Distinguishes claims of logical error from claims of moral disagreement
Reaches and justifies an overall verdict

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Aristotle's conception of justice as proportion with Kant's 'end in himself' and Bentham's utilitarian equality, and assess which, if any, better handles cases where two people's interests or claims conflict.
rubric: Identifies the specific difficulty Russell raises for Kant's view
Uses at least one concrete example from the chapter (e.g. master/slave, husband/wife)
